record.paper_title: Protocols for Observational Studies: Methods and Open Problems
record.context_brief: Reader interpretation of abstracts and conclusions
record.original_question: What empirical evidence is needed about how readers interpret language in abstracts and conclusions, especially when observational studies report nonsignificant primary analyses together with significant secondary analyses, so that reporting guidance can reduce selective interpretation of study findings?

evidence.quote: In this conclusion, did we pay too much heed to a secondary analysis finding? Did we selectively interpret the findings? It would be useful to have more empirical research on how readers interpret language in abstracts and conclusions of papers.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Design and carry out an empirical research program to characterize how readers of scientific literature interpret the language used in the abstracts and conclusions of observational studies, with particular attention to the case in which a study reports a nonsignificant result for its primary analysis alongside a statistically significant result for one or more secondary analyses. Specifically:

(a) Develop reproducible measurements (e.g., randomized reader experiments, surveys, eye-tracking, or structured comprehension assessments) that quantify the inferences readers draw about overall study findings, causal claims, and the relative weight given to primary versus secondary analyses, as a function of specific wording choices in abstracts and concluding paragraphs.

(b) Identify which linguistic patterns (hedging, ordering of findings, emphasis on secondary results, framing of nonsignificance, etc.) systematically increase the probability of selective interpretation, defined as readers giving disproportionate weight to secondary significant findings relative to a nonsignificant primary analysis.

(c) From this evidence, derive concrete reporting guidance—e.g., rules for the structure and wording of abstracts and conclusions of observational studies—that demonstrably reduces selective interpretation, and validate the effectiveness of this guidance through controlled comparison against current reporting practices.

Provide the empirical evidence base needed to support such guidance.
artifact.category_tag: reporting and interpretation in observational studies
artifact.status_search_result: Existing meta-epidemiological studies document widespread misinterpretation of nonsignificant results and over-representation of significant p-values in abstracts (in RCTs, Cochrane reviews, and surgical trials), but no dedicated empirical research program targets how readers process the combination of nonsignificant primary and significant secondary analyses in observational studies, nor evaluates reporting guidance designed to mitigate this selective interpretation. The question therefore remains open as a research agenda.

status_evidence.title: A review of high impact journals found that misinterpretation of non-statistically significant results from randomized trials was common
status_evidence.snippet: Of 50 RCTs with non-statistically significant primary outcomes, 56% of abstracts concluded there was no difference; 38% over-emphasized statistical significance.
status_evidence.claim: Misinterpretation of nonsignificant results in abstracts is empirically documented but not resolved by reporting guidance.

status_evidence.title: The over-representation of significant p values in abstracts compared to corresponding full texts
status_evidence.snippet: Outcomes reported in abstracts had three times the odds of being significant than in full texts.
status_evidence.claim: Selective emphasis on significant findings in abstracts is widespread, motivating further empirical study.

status_evidence.title: Beyond statistical significance: nuanced interpretations of statistically nonsignificant results were rare in Cochrane reviews
status_evidence.snippet: Nuanced interpretation of nonsignificant findings is rare even in Cochrane reviews.
status_evidence.claim: Empirical reader-interpretation work and evidence-based reporting guidance for nonsignificant primary plus significant secondary results remain lacking.
